episode_title: The WRONG Way to Fight Extremists

stories.topic: Solving the Eight Queens Problem in a Feverish Sitting
stories.summary: After many years, Amit picked up the chessboard, set up the eight queens puzzle (place eight queens so that none can capture another), and cracked it 'in one feverish attempt' — having last solved it twenty years ago. Ajay's response: he has lost the ability to think of it as a chess problem at all; for him it is the n-queens problem, an algorithm to be written in Fortran (then nicer languages), and the only interesting question is how to generate all solutions for arbitrary n.
stories.insight: Same puzzle, two cognitive worlds. Amit gets the satisfaction of human-scale problem-solving; Ajay sees only the meta-question — the general algorithm. A small portrait of how a long programming life rewires what a 'problem' even means.

stories.topic: OPEC, the Cartoon Cartel That Couldn't
stories.summary: OPEC was the most brazen cartel ever — a coalition of governments (so beyond antitrust reach) coordinating to fix the oil price. Furious after losing the 1973 war to Israel, they cut production by just 8% and the price went from $1.50 to $11. Yet from 1974 to 2023 — nearly fifty years — crude oil rose only about 1.5% per year in real terms. Ajay traces the failure to four forces: long-run elasticity (efficiency, alternatives), countries refusing to be extorted (Henry Kissinger reportedly authored a pseudonymous article sketching a military operation to seize the Persian Gulf), cheating by members with large populations (Iraq, Iran flooding the market when Saudi Arabia tried to cut), and political incoherence inside the bloc.
stories.insight: The most cartoonish cartel in modern history delivered 1.5% real over fifty years. Cartels collapse under their own incentives — high prices unlock alternatives, members defect, and victims build escape routes. A monopoly without state-enforced barriers to entry is a monopoly with a countdown timer.

stories.topic: Reverse OPEC — When India and China Became the Buyers' Cartel
stories.summary: When the Ukraine war began in February 2022, Putin tried to extort Europe by choking gas — assuming Europe would freeze and fold. Europe called the bluff and rapidly restructured its energy system. Russian crude shifted to India and China. Then the West invented an audacious new tool: a $60-per-barrel price cap, enforced not on Russia or its buyers but on the Western-dominated shipping and insurance industries (you couldn't ship or insure Russian oil above $60). With Putin desperate for war funding and only two large buyers left, India and China became a 'reverse OPEC' — a cartel of buyers driving the price down.
stories.insight: A perfect role-reversal. The seller's cartel of the 1970s became the buyer's cartel of the 2020s. Power flowed not to whoever owned the resource but to whoever owned the chokepoint — and Western dominance of shipping insurance turned out to be a bigger lever than anyone expected.

stories.summary: After recording an episode with Ramachandra Guha in Bangalore's Church Street, Amit told Guha he was off to 'the best bookshop in the world' — Blossoms. Guha, in Amit's paraphrase: 'You fool, you know nothing. Blossoms is not even the best bookshop on Church Street,' and dragged him to a shop called Bookworm. Amit visited both. Bookworm happened to stock 'a shitty book I wrote a decade and a half ago,' so he immediately concluded Blossoms was better.
stories.insight: A warm, self-deprecating moment about being humbled by an erudite friend — and about the small, biased loyalties (your own book on the shelf!) that survive any amount of intellectual humility. Also a love letter to Blossoms' third-floor secondhand section, the kind of bookshop a person would happily spend a week in instead of going to Bali.

stories.topic: The Kashmiri Boy Whose Brother Disappeared
stories.summary: Amit asks the listener to imagine the world from a young Kashmiri boy's point of view: his older brother taken away by security forces, never to return; his sister blinded out on the streets; ordinary life impossible without paying a bribe to someone in uniform. From inside that life, how could he not feel alienated from the state? David Devadas's *A Generation of Rage* documents 2007 as a window of hope — a generation that wanted to be engineers, programmers, artists — squandered by an entrenched security apparatus running on perverse incentives (head-count rewards, rent-seeking, casual extortion).
stories.insight: Counterinsurgency that creates more militants than it kills is a doomed enterprise. The Indian state in Kashmir was 100% military and 0% political — and so it manufactured the next generation of insurgents one alienated boy at a time. Saying 'Kashmir is an integral part of India' implies Kashmiris are Indians; treating them as enemies turns the slogan into a lie.

stories.topic: Decalogue I — The Father Who Calculated the Ice
stories.summary: In Krzysztof Kieslowski's *Decalogue I* (on the commandment 'Thou shalt have no other god before me'), an ultra-rational scientist father — monitoring temperatures, weather reports, every variable — calculates the precise day his young son can safely skate on the frozen lake. He gets the math right within margin of error. The boy goes skating. The ice cracks. He dies. The film closes on the father by the lake, with a homeless man in the distance who has lit a fire.
stories.insight: Not an anti-science message, Amit insists, but a humility message — the world is too complex to be fully gridded by any model, and the engineering mindset that thinks otherwise courts tragedy. The lit fire in the distance is the haunting counterpoint to the father's calculations: warmth, ritual, the inscrutable, persisting beside a rationality that just collapsed.

stories.topic: Show Don't Tell — A Short Film About Love
stories.summary: Amit teaches his writing students 'show don't tell' through a scene from Kieslowski's *A Short Film About Love*. A young man secretly in love with a woman in the building opposite finally rings her doorbell, intending to ask her out. A conventional film would cut to the door opening, the dialogue, her reaction. Kieslowski instead cuts straight to the boy down in the courtyard riding his bicycle in tight, ecstatic circles — and in that one shot, with no dialogue, you know exactly what happened.
stories.insight: The cleanest demonstration of why 'show don't tell' is more than a writing maxim — it's about trusting the audience's intelligence. The image of joy is more efficient (and more beautiful) than the depicted joy. The negative space is doing the work.

recommendations.creator: Adam Smith
recommendations.context: Smith's 1776 foundational text of modern economics.
recommendations.reason: Source of the show's framing line for the episode: 'People of the same trade seldom meet together, even for merriment and diversion, but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices.' The intuition for why cartels are an ever-present temptation — and for why competition is the only real defence.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's five-hour-plus deep dive with Ajay on the Russia-Ukraine war.
recommendations.reason: Recommended as the long-form companion to the cartel discussion — for the deeper geopolitical and economic mechanics of the war that turned OPEC's logic on its head.

recommendations.item: The Insurgents: David Petraeus and the Plot to Change the American Way of War
recommendations.creator: Fred Kaplan
recommendations.context: How a small group of soldier-intellectuals, led by Petraeus, dragged American military doctrine away from pure lethality toward counterinsurgency.
recommendations.reason: Amit's accidental entry point — picked up on a Blossoms hardback sale shelf — that became the rabbit hole for this entire chapter. It contains Kaplan's clean summary of David Galula's five-step process, and is the modern bridge to the older counterinsurgency canon.

recommendations.creator: David Galula
recommendations.context: The 1960s Bible of counterinsurgency, written by a French officer who fought (and was once imprisoned by) Mao's men in China and then fought in Algeria.
recommendations.reason: The foundational text. Source of the fly-and-lion metaphor and the five-step framework: concentrate force to push insurgents out, hold the area, make contact with the people and earn their trust, destroy the insurgent political organisation and replace it with a legitimate one, mop up the remnants. Every later counterinsurgency thinker is in conversation with Galula.

recommendations.creator: T. E. Lawrence
recommendations.context: Lawrence of Arabia's memoir of leading the Arab Revolt against the Ottomans in WWI.
recommendations.reason: Source of the line that has come to define how counterinsurgency feels in practice — that doing it conventionally is 'like eating soup with a knife.' Awkward, slow, and shaped wrong for the work.

recommendations.item: Learning to Eat Soup with a Knife: Counterinsurgency Lessons from Malaya and Vietnam
recommendations.creator: John Nagl
recommendations.context: Nagl's study of why the British army learned in Malaya and the American army didn't in Vietnam.
recommendations.reason: The institutional-learning question — why some militaries absorb lessons and others don't. Pairs naturally with Galula and Kaplan: Galula tells you what to do, Nagl tells you why your organisation will probably refuse to do it.

recommendations.item: The Generation of Rage in Kashmir
recommendations.creator: David Devadas
recommendations.context: A reported account of how a generation of Kashmiris turned from possible reconciliation to renewed insurgency.
recommendations.reason: Devadas's contention is that 2007 was a year of new beginnings — a generation wanting jobs, normal lives, careers in tech and the arts — squandered by an entrenched security state running on perverse incentives (head-count rewards, rent-seeking, casual extortion of anyone making money). The most concrete account Amit has read of how political failure created the next wave of militants.

recommendations.item: India, Pakistan, Kashmir: We Won't Need To Fight A War If We Can Win The Peace
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's BloombergQuint column applying the counterinsurgency lens to India's Kashmir policy.
recommendations.reason: His own crystallisation of the Galula-Petraeus argument as it applies to India: if Kashmir is an integral part of India, Kashmiris are Indians, and the state's job is to serve them — not to occupy them.

recommendations.item: A Tale Of Two Bandits: Naxals And The Indian State
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's BloombergQuint column applying Mancur Olson's stationary/roving bandit framework to the Naxal conflict.
recommendations.reason: Argues that in many Naxal-affected areas, both the state and the Naxalites have behaved as roving bandits — and in some pockets it was the Naxals who tried to settle in, tax sustainably, and provide services. Reframes the conflict from a law-and-order problem into a legitimacy problem.

recommendations.creator: Mancur Olson
recommendations.context: Olson's foundational work on group behaviour, free-riding, and the conditions under which groups can act in their collective interest.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 'roving bandits vs. stationary bandits' frame that anchors Amit's Naxal analysis — and a deeper general lens for understanding when collective action succeeds and fails.

recommendations.item: The Indian Armed Forces (Episode 175, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lt Gen Prakash Menon
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Lt Gen Prakash Menon, who once commanded the army in Kashmir.
recommendations.reason: Where Amit got the inside-the-institution view of Kashmir — defensive, coherent, and a good test of his own framing. Menon's reaction ('we did everything right; what are we to do if Pakistan sends its people?') captures exactly the worldview the episode is critiquing.

recommendations.item: The Liberal Nationalism of Nitin Pai (Episode 318, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Nitin Pai
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive with strategic thinker Nitin Pai.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Amit had a strong argument with Pai on the same Kashmir/national-security questions. Recommended as the long-form back-and-forth on the tension between defending borders and treating one's own citizens as one's own.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 'failures of state capability are not domain-specific, they are cross-cutting' idea: the same missing feedback loops break Indian health, finance, security, and monetary policy alike.

recommendations.creator: Tirthankar Roy
recommendations.context: Tirthankar Roy's history of Indian business at the interface of business and history.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's book pick of the week. The takeaway that struck him: how little has fundamentally changed in Indian business over a hundred and fifty years. Reading it left him with a new respect for entrepreneurs of a century ago. A book Ajay urges even people who 'have never read a book before' to read for the larger strategic sense.

recommendations.creator: Krzysztof Kieslowski
recommendations.context: A series of ten roughly hour-long films, each loosely inspired by one of the Ten Commandments, made by Kieslowski for Polish television in the late 1980s.
recommendations.reason: Amit's 'pinnacle of cinematic storytelling.' He calls it greater than Kieslowski's later, more famous *Three Colors* trilogy and *The Double Life of Veronique*. The films are not didactic about the commandments — they are beautiful, ambiguous human stories that ask the moral question and leave you with it. *Decalogue I* alone (the father, the son, the ice) is a complete masterpiece on the limits of rationality.

recommendations.creator: Krzysztof Kieslowski
recommendations.context: The feature-length expansion of Decalogue VI.
recommendations.reason: Contains the bicycle-in-the-courtyard scene that Amit uses to teach 'show don't tell' in his writing classes — a single shot that conveys, without dialogue, everything about a young man's first attempt at love. A masterclass in cinematic compression.

recommendations.creator: Krzysztof Kieslowski
recommendations.context: The feature-length expansion of Decalogue V.
recommendations.reason: The other feature-length expansion from the Decalogue cycle. Recommended alongside *A Short Film About Love* as the second self-contained masterpiece spun out of the larger ten-film work.

core_ideas.concept: A Cartel Without State Backing Has a Countdown Timer
core_ideas.explanation: Cartels and seeming monopolies cannot sustain themselves in markets with free entry. When prices rise, alternatives emerge, exploration is funded, members cheat, and victims build escape routes. The only durable monopolies are those propped up by state coercion. Even OPEC — the most cartoonish, brazen cartel in modern history, immune to antitrust because its members were sovereign states — managed only ~1.5% real price growth over 50 years.
core_ideas.quote: A seeming monopoly is impossible to sustain. The only times monopolies or cartels form is when the state actually interferes to give someone an advantage.

core_ideas.explanation: Demand for commodities like crude oil is highly inelastic in the short run — you still drive to work, you still heat your home — so a sudden price shock looks like proof of cartel power. But in the long run, humans adjust dramatically: efficient cars, alternative fuels, new exploration, structural redesign. Most 'permanent' choke-points dissolve over a decade. Reasoning from short-run elasticity to long-run politics is one of the great recurring mistakes in policy.

Hard power through resource control is a self-eroding asset. The moment you weaponise dependence — Russia choking European gas, China choking Japan's rare earths in 2012, the imagined Indian state cutting off JP Morgan's call centres — the victim, no matter how dependent, mobilises every resource to escape. The first three weeks are devastating; the next three years are a strategic disaster for the extortioner. 'In a conflict the other guy gets a vote.'
core_ideas.quote: The moment you try to misbehave and exert your might, then a large scale of responses comes back at you. Nobody likes to be extorted.

core_ideas.concept: Reverse OPEC — Power Flows to the Chokepoint
core_ideas.explanation: After Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the seller's cartel logic flipped. Russian crude could only be sold to two large buyers (India, China), so they became a buyers' cartel. Then the West innovated a new statecraft tool: not sanctioning Russia or its customers, but sanctioning the Western-dominated shipping and insurance industries — capping the price at which they could move or insure Russian oil. Power didn't flow to whoever owned the resource; it flowed to whoever owned the bottleneck. A new template for economic statecraft.

core_ideas.concept: Price Is the Word the Doomsayers Forget
core_ideas.explanation: The Club of Rome's 1972 report mechanically extrapolated resource consumption and predicted catastrophe. The single missing word was 'price.' Once a price system mediates supply and demand, scarcity is self-correcting: higher prices unlock exploration, conservation, substitution, and innovation. Peak Oil failed for the same reason. Worries about lithium monopolies, rare earth chokeholds, and so on tend to fail for the same reason. The constraint that genuinely matters is the one without a price signal — climate change, where we dump CO2 into a commons that doesn't bill us.
core_ideas.quote: What was missing in that entire thinking was the word price.

core_ideas.explanation: The line attributed to one of Mao's generals; the operating principle behind Galula, Petraeus, and the modern counterinsurgency canon. Conventional military force can secure terrain but cannot create legitimacy. Without local trust, every militant you kill creates more than one new one. Galula's five-step recipe — concentrate force, hold the area, earn the people's trust, replace the insurgents' political organisation with a legitimate one, mop up — is fundamentally a political programme that uses the military as one instrument among several.
core_ideas.quote: Will this operation take more bad guys off the street than it creates by the way it's conducted? — David Petraeus

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's mathematical re-statement of the Petraeus question. COVID taught everyone the basic reproduction number: if R0 > 1 the epidemic explodes. The same logic applies to militancy — if killing one militant creates 1.01 militants on average, the insurgency grows without bound. Every operation should be evaluated by its effect on the militant R0, not by body count. Most counterinsurgencies fail because they optimise the wrong metric.
core_ideas.quote: If in the process of killing one militant you create 1.01 militants on average, then you've had it because this thing will explode.

core_ideas.explanation: Galula's metaphor: a fly and a lion fighting. The fly cannot deliver a knockout blow; the lion cannot swat the fly. A fly-swatter doesn't help — the flies just keep coming. Conventional military doctrine, designed for war between states with defined territories and armies, is structurally mis-shaped for fighting insurgents who blend into a civilian population. Different war, different tools, different rules of engagement.

Mancur Olson's model. A roving bandit robs a village and leaves; he extracts everything because he isn't coming back. A stationary bandit settles in and rules; he extracts sustainably because the people are a renewable resource — he taxes them, so he must build infrastructure, provide some services, prevent rival bandits. A state, in this view, is the stationary bandit who has won. In many of India's Naxal areas, both the state and the Naxalites have behaved as roving bandits — and in some pockets the Naxals have been the better stationary bandit, providing services the state didn't.
core_ideas.quote: People are resources that create more.

core_ideas.concept: Don't Use a Military Machine on Your Own Citizens
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's sharp restatement: a military is an institution designed to marshal unlimited, unbelievable levels of violence against an enemy. Its tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) are calibrated for that. Pointing that machine inward — at one's own population — is structurally dangerous. The lethality that makes an army useful for war makes it disastrous for policing. The line between external war-fighting and internal security is one of the most important lines a republic maintains.

When 'national security' becomes a trump card, debate stops. The argument 'we had to do X because of terrorists' is a checkmate move that disables the cost-benefit reasoning a republic needs. Ajay extends the diagnosis: it's not unique to security policy. The same checkmate operates in financial policy ('crisis!'), in pandemic policy, in any domain where fear can be mobilised. Fear is the surest path to bad policy.

core_ideas.concept: War Is Too Important to Be Left to the Generals
core_ideas.explanation: If only security professionals debate security, the Republic gets worse decisions. The Western counterinsurgency revolution happened because soldier-intellectuals like Galula and Petraeus broke the closed loop — bringing in history, social science, philosophy, criticism. India's failures in Kashmir partly stem from the absence of that intellectual ecosystem. The same diagnosis (per Kelkar-Shah's *In Service of the Republic*) applies to Indian health, finance, and almost every domain: the missing piece is feedback loops, criticism, postmortems, evidence — what they call the intellectual capacity of the state.

core_ideas.concept: The Western Way of War Is the Western Way of Introspection
core_ideas.explanation: What is striking about Western military culture, Ajay argues, is its relentless self-examination — diaries, after-action reports, books, mournful memoirs, intellectual debates about what went wrong. That literature is the substrate on which militaries get better. The Indian state — and Indian institutions broadly — lack this culture of introspection. That's the middle-income trap of capability: you can mobilise resources, but you can't compound learning.

Kieslowski's image of the rational father whose perfect calculation kills his son is a humility lesson, not an anti-science one. The world is too complex to be fully captured by any model; the engineering mindset that imagines otherwise is dangerous precisely because of its competence. The lit fire by the homeless man at the end of the film is the counterpoint — warmth, ritual, the inscrutable, persisting beside collapsed rationality.

The bicycle scene from *A Short Film About Love* as the cleanest demonstration of the principle. A conventional director would show the doorbell, the conversation, the rejection. Kieslowski cuts to the boy spinning ecstatic circles in the courtyard — and the audience knows everything. Trust the audience; let the negative space do the work; the depicted thing is almost always smaller than the thing implied.

Amit's mini-rant from his five years as a professional poker player. Gambling, properly defined, is sussing up probabilities and making a bet. By that definition, every consequential act in life is a gamble — talking to a stranger in a bar, buying a 'haunted' house at a discount, launching a podcast. Treating gambling as a moral category misses that risk-taking is the substrate of being alive. Ajay's counter: lotteries (negative expected value) and excessive financial leverage are decision mistakes, but not properly the state's business — caveat emptor.
core_ideas.quote: Lotteries are taxes on people who are bad at math.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay on the eight queens problem: he has lost the ability to think of it as a chess problem at all — for him it's the n-queens algorithm. Amit's deadpan reaction: 'When AI can do this, why are you wasting your time?'

Amit on Bookworm vs. Blossoms: Ramachandra Guha drags him to a rival bookshop on Church Street to prove a point. Bookworm turns out to stock 'a shitty book I wrote a decade and a half ago,' so Amit immediately rules in favour of Blossoms. Self-interest, gracefully admitted.
Ajay's one-liner that Putin should get the Nobel Peace Prize for solving climate change — by accidentally forcing Europe into a renewable-energy sprint.

Ajay on the Bollywood-isation of resource economics — 'Boss, mai batata hoon, there's a Bollywood film in this. Lithium' — only to have Amit point out lithium is plentiful in the universe (made in stellar furnaces right after hydrogen and helium). Ajay then casts about the periodic table for a properly scarce element to base the film on: 'tantalum,' or one of the rare earths with beautiful names like yttrium.

Ajay's call-centre thought experiment for hard power: imagine the Indian state forced every Indian call centre to refuse JP Morgan. 'It would be a big disruption for JP Morgan for the first three weeks. And then in the long run, by God the world will find ways to get their call-centre work done without dealing with somebody who misbehaves.'
Amit signs off the gambling rant: 'Thank you for watching. It's been a gamble on your part to watch it — and if you're still here, you've enjoyed it. So well done, you're a gambler.'

Adam Smith's line — 'People of the same trade seldom meet together, even for merriment and diversion, but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices' — invoked as the show's mental model for why cartels are an ever-present temptation.

Ahmed Zaki Yamani, the legendary Saudi oil minister: 'The Stone Age did not end because the world ran out of stones.' Used as the prophetic line about the inevitable end of the oil age — not by depletion but by substitution. Yamani himself, Ajay notes, was probably picturing nuclear fusion (which has always been the technology of the next twenty years and probably always will be); decarbonisation is the substitute that actually arrived.

Henry Kissinger reportedly authored a pseudonymous magazine article in the 1970s sketching a military operation to seize the oil fields of the Persian Gulf and turn them into a 'global trust' — a reminder that even the cartoonishly powerful OPEC operated under the threat that powerful consumers might just take their oil.
T. E. Lawrence's image of counterinsurgency as 'eating soup with a knife' — awkward, slow, shaped wrong for the work. John Nagl borrowed it as the title of his book on military learning.
One of Mao's generals on the ratio that defines counterinsurgency: '20% military, 80% political.' The line that organises Amit's whole chapter.

Ariel Sharon's name for the 1967 Arab-Israeli war: the Six-Day War. Cited as the prelude to the 1973 war — the strategic surprise the Arab world prepared for, lost again, and then redirected its rage into the OPEC oil shock.
Bob Dylan's 'A Hard Rain's A-Gonna Fall' — gestured at by Amit as the rain pours outside during recording: 'one of our heroes, Bob Dylan — a hard rain's a-gonna fall.'
The 1972 Club of Rome report — the canonical example of mechanical doom-extrapolation that ignored the price system. Invoked as the warning against any contemporary 'we'll run out of X' panic.
